readerTitle: Why great businesses keep a 'no' list
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주방용품 매장, 사내 디자인팀) + 실제 기업 (1997년 Apple 제품 라인 정리) · 매장 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 전략은 무엇을 할지보다 무엇을 하지 않을지로 더 분명해진다. '아니오'는 손실이 아니라 핵심에 쓸 자원을 되찾는 일이다.
misconception: 더 많은 제품, 고객, 요청에 '예'라고 할수록 매출과 기회가 늘어난다.

sources.text: Porter, M. (1996). What Is Strategy? Harvard Business Review. ("The essence of strategy is choosing what not to do.")
Isaacson, W. (2011). Steve Jobs. Simon & Schuster. (1997년 Apple 제품 라인을 4칸 그리드로 정리한 과정)
주방용품 매장과 사내 디자인팀 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 매장 계산: 연매출 $2,000,000 중 하위 1,000개 제품 매출 $80,000 = 4%. 재고 $120,000(원가 기준)는 가정값. 3,000개 중 1,000개 = 1/3. 모든 수치는 가상입니다.
Porter(1996) 인용문 "The essence of strategy is choosing what not to do"의 정확한 문구를 원문에서 확인하세요.
Apple이 1997년 잡스 복귀 후 제품 라인을 소비자/프로 × 데스크톱/노트북 4칸으로 줄였다는 내용은 Isaacson 전기 등으로 확인하세요. 줄인 제품 수나 비율은 자료마다 달라 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다. 이후 실적 회복은 여러 요인이 겹친 결과라 '그 결정 하나 덕분'이라고 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: A store removed a third of its products. Sales went up.
body: Picture a kitchen-supply store with 3,000 products on its shelves. The owner cuts 1,000 of them.
It sounds like throwing away sales. The numbers tell a different story, and it's a story about what strategy really is.

image.label: Crowded store shelves next to clean, well-stocked ones
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽은 잡다한 주방용품이 빽빽하게 뒤엉킨 선반, 오른쪽은 같은 크기 선반에 업소용 냄비와 칼이 넉넉하게 채워진 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Sales are flat and shelves are packed.
body: Your store sells to home cooks and local restaurants. Restaurants bring in most of your sales, but their buyers complain that the items they need are often out of stock.
You carry 3,000 products. What do you do?

options.text: Add 500 new products to attract more home cooks
options.feedback: You might win a few new shoppers, but shelves, cash and staff time get stretched even thinner. Your best customers would wait even longer.

options.text: Drop the 1,000 slowest products and stock deeper on what restaurants buy
options.feedback: You give up some small sales to fix the problem your biggest customers care about. The next card shows how small those sales are.

options.text: Discount the slow products to clear space, then reorder them
options.feedback: It frees space for a while, but you'll buy the same products again. The clutter comes back because nothing was actually decided.

cards.title: What the slowest third really brings in.
body: Cutting them gives up **$80,000** a year. In return you get back a third of your shelves, $120,000 in cash and hours of ordering every week. All of it can go to the customers who matter most.

breakdown.label: Shelf space
breakdown.detail: Room your best sellers don't get

cards.title: Choosing what not to do
body: **Choosing what not to do** means deciding, on purpose, which products, customers and activities you will turn down so your limited resources go to what matters most.
Michael Porter put it plainly in his 1996 essay "What Is Strategy?": the essence of strategy is choosing what not to do.
Every yes uses up shelf space, cash, people or attention. A 'no' list protects them.

image.label: A short 'yes' list beside a longer 'no' list
image.brief: 메모지 두 장. 왼쪽 "We do"에 3줄, 오른쪽 "We don't"에 5줄이 손글씨로 적혀 있음. 오른쪽 메모지가 더 길어 보이게.

cards.title: Apple's four-box grid.
body: When Steve Jobs returned to Apple in 1997, the company was losing money and selling many overlapping computer models. Customers struggled to tell them apart.
He cut the line down to a simple grid of four: a desktop and a laptop, each for consumers and for professionals. Everything outside the four boxes was dropped.
Saying no made the remaining products easier to build, sell and explain.
cards.softwareNote: In software, each feature you say yes to has to be maintained, tested and supported for years. A written list of features you won't build is often worth more than a long roadmap.

cards.title: You can say no to more than products.
body: A 'no' list can name customers you won't chase, services you won't offer and channels you won't sell through.
A cleaning company might say no to one-off jobs and focus on regular contracts. A bakery might say no to custom cakes so mornings stay fast.
A clear list also helps staff. They can turn down a poor fit without asking the owner every time.

cards.title: Some 'no's cost more than they look.
body: A slow product can still matter. If restaurants come in for one rare item and fill a whole basket while they're there, cutting it may lose the basket.
Saying no also means some customers will leave. That's the price of focus, so decide it on purpose.
And a 'no' list isn't forever. Review it when your customers or costs change.

cards.title: Now it's a design team inside a manufacturer.
body: Your four-person design team gets requests from six departments: product launches, trade-show booths, internal posters, one-off flyers and slides. Launch work keeps slipping.
What do you do?

options.text: Say yes to everything and add weekend hours
options.feedback: Everyone gets an answer, but launches stay late and the team burns out. Nothing was chosen, so nothing improves.

options.text: Publish what the team will and won't do, and point simple requests to templates
options.feedback: Some departments lose custom work, but launches get the time they need. A clear list also ends the daily arguments over priority.

options.text: Handle requests in the order they arrive
options.feedback: It feels fair and needs no debate. But a poster that arrives first still beats a launch that matters more.

cards.title: Your strategy is as clear as your 'no' list.
body: Every yes uses resources your core work needs. Choosing what to turn down is how you protect it.
**Try it today:** write three things your business will stop doing or stop offering. Note what each one frees up.
